analysis.title: Anatomy of a Crash: Lessons From 2000
key_insights: The Nasdaq peaked on March 10, 2000 and lost more than a third of its value by mid-April. The S&P 500 stayed resilient and was still near record highs six months after the Nasdaq peak. Broad-market pressure arrived only when the economic outlook deteriorated.

After the initial drop, the Nasdaq rallied 35% from its lows by mid-June 2000, leaving it 15% below the March peak. Dip buying was supported by strong earnings expectations and a decade of rewarded dip buyers.
Money rotated from speculative dotcom names into profitable tech leaders (Cisco, Oracle, Intel, Microsoft). The report says this quality trade did not protect investors.
Stanley Druckenmiller sold his tech exposure in January 2000, then bought $6 billion of tech stocks in March near the top. He lost $3 billion within six weeks.

Tech demand data lagged the price peak. Semiconductor sales kept rising after the Nasdaq peaked, backlogs stayed elevated and shortages persisted. Within six months shortages turned into a glut. Greenspan cited strong capex and tech demand in autumn 2000.

Unprofitable dotcoms were hit first as IPO funding and credit tightened. They were also key customers of Cisco, Lucent and Nortel, so the loss of external financing cut demand across the ecosystem. Earnings downgrades then spread to the companies seen as safe. The report compares this to the current debate over AI spending sustainability.

TS Lombard says today's multiples are well below 2000 extremes, but the larger risk is whether earnings assumptions can be sustained. Late-1990s corporate profit data were later revised significantly lower.
Technicals: SPX is testing the 7,300 support area again, having tested it repeatedly since June. A break would put 7,000 in focus. NDX and SOX are below their 200-day moving averages.

The report says the AI boom has not necessarily ended. Hyperscaler capex plans and compute demand remain strong and another rebound is possible. In 2000 the market fell well before fundamentals visibly deteriorated, and strong fundamentals did not prevent the crash.
risk_factors: Earnings assumptions for AI-related companies may not be sustainable, even though multiples are below 2000 levels.
Customer financing risk: AI spending may depend on external financing, as dotcom customers did, and a funding squeeze could cut demand across the ecosystem.
Market declines can precede visible fundamental deterioration, and demand and backlog data can lag.
Technical break of SPX 7,300 support, with 7,000 as the next area.
vol_and_positioning: SPX has repeatedly tested the 7,300 support area since June, which raises the risk of an eventual break. A move below puts 7,000 in focus.
NDX and SOX trade below their 200-day moving averages.

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscaler capex plans remain strong, compute demand is robust, another rebound remains possible, and multiples are far below 2000 extremes.
tension_points.bear_case: In 2000 the market fell well before fundamentals deteriorated, and earnings downgrades came later after major damage. The larger risk now is that earnings assumptions cannot be sustained, and AI spending may depend on external financing.
tension_points.what_invalidates: SPX break below the 7,300 support area, with 7,000 in focus.

theme_stances.key_argument: In 2000 the market started falling long before fundamentals visibly deteriorated, and strong fundamentals did not prevent the crash.
theme_stances.evidence: Strong fundamentals didn't prevent the crash in 2000.
